title: Regression & Predictive Modeling
excerpt: Regression summarizes how an outcome changes with one or more measured factors, while accounting for the other factors included in the model. Learn to interpret coefficients and predictions, check how well a model fits, and see why a relationship is not automatically a cause—with examples such as wages, prices and policy outcomes.
objectives: Interpret intercepts and slopes in the units of the response and predictor.
Calculate fitted values and residuals, and use diagnostic plots to assess linearity, variance, dependence, leverage and outliers.
Distinguish association, prediction and causal interpretation in financial regression.
Compare confidence intervals for mean responses with prediction intervals for individual outcomes.
Evaluate statistical evidence with effect size, uncertainty, validation performance and practical importance rather than R-squared alone.

lessons.title: Start with a question, units and a fitted line
lessons.body:
Regression asks how an outcome changes on average with a predictor. In the simple model, ŷ = b₀ + b₁x, ŷ is the fitted response, x is the predictor, b₀ is the intercept and b₁ is the slope. The slope's units are response units per predictor unit; the intercept is the fitted response when x = 0, which may be outside the useful data range. For an illustrative dataset, x = 1, 2, 3 and y = 2, 3, 5, least squares gives approximately ŷ = 0.33 + 1.50x. At x = 4, the fitted value is 6.33 response units. These numbers are simulated for teaching, not historical evidence.

Read a fitted line as a compact summary of the sample, not as a rule for every person. Imagine a teaching model for weekly earnings: predicted pay = £300 + £25 × years of schooling. At 12 years the model predicts £300 + 12 × £25 = £600; at 13 years it predicts £625. The slope, £25 per year, is the model’s average difference in predicted pay for a one-year difference in schooling over the data being modelled. The £300 intercept is the model’s predicted value at zero years; if the data contain no such cases, it may be only a mathematical anchor rather than a useful real-world prediction.

The line describes a conditional average, so individual people can earn more or less; their residual is observed pay minus predicted pay. A straight-line summary can miss curves, and predictions far outside the observed schooling range are extrapolations. Most importantly, people with more schooling may also differ in family background, prior opportunity or other factors, so the slope is not automatically the causal payoff to an extra year. Check residuals and the sample range, and use a credible design for causal claims. See the NIST regression references and Angrist & Pischke Chapter 3 linked below.

Before fitting, identify what one row represents and keep the time unit fixed. Suppose a synthetic sample records quarterly household spending in dollars and hours worked per week: a fitted line is spending = 420 dollars + 18 dollars per weekly hour. For a household working 30 hours, the arithmetic is 420 dollars + (18 dollars/hour × 30 hours) = 960 dollars per quarter. Raising hours from 30 to 32 changes the fitted value by 2 × 18 = 36 dollars per quarter, not 36 percent. This is an average comparison within the observed range, assuming the linear summary is reasonable and measurements are comparable. It does not show that adding work hours causes spending to rise; income, household size, and other factors may differ. For an introduction to fitting and interpreting a linear regression, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 8: Introduction to Linear Regression’ in the linked sources.

Consider a new illustrative, synthetic fund example with the fitted line ŷ = 0.20 pp + 0.80 (fund pp per market pp) × x, where x is the market’s monthly excess return. If the market return is 1.50%, use percentage points consistently: x = 1.50 pp. The fitted fund excess return is 0.20 pp + 0.80 × 1.50 pp = 1.40 pp. If the synthetic observed fund return is 2.10 pp, its residual is observed minus fitted = 2.10 pp − 1.40 pp = +0.70 pp; the fund exceeded the line’s conditional average for that month. For a market return of −1.00 pp, the fitted value is 0.20 − 0.80 = −0.60 pp, not −0.60%. Thus the slope implies a fitted change of 0.80 pp for each 1 pp change in the market, while the intercept is evaluated at zero market excess return. This assumes both series use the same monthly window and definitions. A residual is unexplained sample deviation, not evidence of a causal mechanism or a reliable next-month forecast; serial dependence, omitted factors and changing volatility may still matter.
lessons.takeaway: Name the observational unit, time window and units before interpreting a coefficient.
lessons.formula: ŷ = b₀ + b₁x; b₀ = intercept, b₁ = slope, x = predictor, ŷ = fitted outcome.

practice.question: Using ŷ = 0.33 + 1.50x, what is the fitted outcome when x = 4, and what are its units?
practice.hint: Substitute x = 4 and keep the response-unit-per-predictor-unit meaning of the slope visible.
practice.solution: ŷ = 0.33 + 1.50(4) = 6.33, so the fitted outcome is about 6.33 response units. It is a model average, not a guaranteed observation.

lessons.title: Calculate residuals and read what they leave behind
lessons.body:
A residual is the observed outcome minus its fitted value: eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ, where yᵢ is observation i and eᵢ is its unexplained remainder under the model. If an observed value is 5.00 and the fitted value is 4.83, the residual is +0.17 response units; the model under-predicted that case. Residual plots should be checked against fitted values, predictors and time order. A curved band suggests nonlinearity, a funnel suggests changing variance, and runs in time suggest dependence. A large residual is not automatically an error: investigate measurement, unusual conditions and influence before deleting it. Least squares minimizes the sum of squared residuals, so extreme residuals receive disproportionate weight.

Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data; monthly units): suppose a simple model uses a town’s average bus fare in January, February and March to predict monthly passenger trips per 1,000 residents. The fitted equation is predicted trips = 12,000 − 300 × fare, where fare is measured in pounds per ride and predicted trips are rides per month. In February, the fare is £2.00 and the observed total is 11,600 rides per 1,000 residents. The fitted value is 12,000 − 300(2.00) = 11,400 rides, so the residual is observed minus fitted = 11,600 − 11,400 = +200 rides per 1,000 residents. The positive residual means February had more trips than this line predicts; it does not by itself explain why.

Use residuals to assess what the fitted line leaves behind, not to prove a policy effect. A useful diagnostic is a residual plot against fitted values, fare or calendar month: a curved pattern suggests that a straight line misses nonlinearity, a funnel shape suggests changing variance, and runs across months may indicate dependence. The calculation also assumes the recorded outcome and fare are measured consistently and that the model form is reasonable over the observed fare range. A common mistake is to call a positive residual a causal impact of cheaper transport; it is only an observed-minus-predicted difference under this model. For diagnostic guidance, see “NIST — Residual Diagnostics” in the linked sources below.

A residual can be compared across cases only when its outcome units are clear. Consider synthetic weekly forecasts of electricity demand in megawatt-hours (MWh): the model predicts 1,250 MWh for week 6, while actual recorded demand is 1,310 MWh. Thus e = 1,310 MWh − 1,250 MWh = +60 MWh, meaning demand exceeded the fitted value by 60 MWh. If another week has a −60 MWh residual, the magnitudes match but the signs show opposite errors. Plotting these residuals in calendar order can reveal a pattern: four positive errors in a row may indicate an omitted seasonal effect. The calculation assumes the same demand definition and forecast horizon for both numbers. It does not identify the cause of the miss or prove a policy effect. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST — Residual Diagnostics’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example (not observed data): standardizing a residual can make its unusualness comparable across periods with different typical error sizes. Suppose a model predicts a retailer’s weekly online orders as 2,400 orders and the observed total is 2,520, so e = 2,520 − 2,400 = +120 orders. If comparable residuals have an estimated residual standard deviation of 80 orders, the rough standardized residual is 120/80 = +1.5 SD. A second week might have a smaller raw miss—560 observed versus 500 fitted, e = +60 orders—but a residual SD of only 20 orders, giving +60/20 = +3.0 SD; diagnostically, that second miss is more unusual relative to its local noise. First verify that both forecasts use the same horizon and order definition, then inspect the corresponding predictor, calendar position and leverage. This scaling is not a new causal effect or a license to delete a point: residual spread may vary with fitted level, and high-leverage observations can make a fitted line and its residual scale look deceptively reassuring. Treat the numbers as a screening aid, then investigate the data-generating conditions.
lessons.takeaway: Residuals reveal systematic structure that the chosen regression form has not captured.
lessons.formula: eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ; eᵢ = residual for observation i, yᵢ = observed outcome, ŷᵢ = fitted outcome.

practice.question: An observed monthly return is 1.2% and its fitted return is 0.8%. What is the residual?
practice.hint: Subtract fitted from observed, retaining percentage-point units.
practice.solution: e = 1.2% − 0.8% = +0.4 percentage points. The positive sign means the observation was above the model's fitted value.

lessons.title: Measure fit without mistaking R-squared for truth
lessons.body:
R-squared summarizes the fraction of in-sample variation around the outcome mean that the fitted model reduces under its definition. A common form is R² = 1 − SSE/SST, where SSE is the sum of squared residuals and SST is the total sum of squared deviations from the sample mean. If SSE = 12 and SST = 20 in an illustrative exercise, R² = 1 − 12/20 = 0.40, or 40%. That does not mean 40% of a future outcome is guaranteed, that the model is correctly specified, or that the relationship is causal. R-squared can rise when variables are added, even if prediction does not improve. Report effect sizes, uncertainty and out-of-sample error too.

R-squared is dimensionless, so it should not be described as 0.40 dollars or 40 percentage points. With synthetic annual-income data, suppose SST = 500,000,000 dollar-squared and SSE = 350,000,000 dollar-squared. Then R² = 1 − 350,000,000/500,000,000 = 1 − 0.70 = 0.30, or 30 percent. The model explains 30 percent of the in-sample squared variation around the sample mean under this calculation; the remaining 70 percent is not a claim that each person is predicted 70 percent incorrectly. A second model might reach R² = 0.35 yet make worse future predictions if it overfits. Interpretation assumes the sums use the same sample and outcome scale. R-squared does not establish causal impact, unbiased forecasts, or practical value. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 8: Introduction to Linear Regression (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.

To test whether fit travels beyond the estimation sample, use a held-out benchmark rather than reading the plotted line as a promise. Suppose six synthetic monthly fund excess returns (in percentage points) are 2, −1, 3, 0, −2, and 1, while a model’s illustrative predictions are 1, 0, 2, 1, −1, and 2. The prediction errors are 1, −1, 1, −1, −1, and −1 pp, so the test SSE is 6 pp² and the test RMSE is √(6/6) = 1 pp per month. A mean-only benchmark predicts the held-out mean, (2 − 1 + 3 + 0 − 2 + 1)/6 = 0.5 pp; its squared deviations sum to 17.5 pp². A test-set R² defined as 1 − SSE_model/SSE_mean is therefore 1 − 6/17.5 = 0.657, or 65.7%. This is a relative score on these six synthetic observations, not a causal effect or a guaranteed future accuracy rate. With a tiny holdout, one unusual month can change it sharply; choose the split chronologically when forecasting time-ordered returns and do not tune the model using the test values.
lessons.takeaway: R-squared is an in-sample summary, not a certificate of correctness, causality or future performance.
lessons.formula: R² = 1 − SSE/SST; SSE = squared residual sum, SST = total squared deviation from the sample mean.

lessons.title: Separate mean-response uncertainty from prediction
lessons.body:
A confidence interval for the mean response describes uncertainty about the average outcome at a chosen predictor value, while a prediction interval describes where one new individual outcome may fall. The latter is wider because it includes both uncertainty in the estimated mean and the new observation's residual variation. For an illustrative forecast at x = 4, suppose the fitted mean is 6.33 units, its 95% confidence interval is 5.80–6.86, and the 95% prediction interval is 3.90–8.76. These are simulated teaching numbers, not a forecast of an asset. State the confidence level, sampling or time-series assumptions, model specification and data range. Do not extrapolate casually beyond observed x values.

Use the interval type that matches the decision. Suppose synthetic data give a fitted mean monthly revenue of 80,000 dollars for stores receiving 10 advertisements, with a 95% confidence interval of 78,000–82,000 dollars. This concerns the average revenue for comparable stores at that advertising level. A 95% prediction interval of 60,000–100,000 dollars concerns one new store and is wider because store-specific variation is included. The midpoint is 80,000 dollars; its half-width is 20,000 dollars, versus 2,000 dollars for the mean interval. These dollar units refer to one month, not an annual total. The interpretation assumes a suitable model, representative sampling, and stable conditions; 95% does not mean this interval has a 95% chance after calculation. Neither interval proves advertising causes revenue. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Penn State STAT 501 — Regression Inference and Prediction Intervals (Lesson 7)’ in the linked sources.

Consider a synthetic weekly-sales regression in which the fitted mean at a discount level observed in the data is 142 units per week. Suppose the residual standard error is 18 units per week, the leverage for this predictor value is h = 0.10, and a teaching approximation uses t = 2.1 for a 95% interval. The confidence interval for the mean is computed as 142 ± 2.1 × 18 × √0.10 = 142 ± 11.95, or approximately 130.0–154.0 units per week. For one new store-week, add the new-outcome noise through √(1 + h): 142 ± 2.1 × 18 × √1.10 = 142 ± 39.64, giving approximately 102.4–181.6 units per week. Thus the prediction interval is wider by design, not because the fitted average changed. This calculation assumes independent, similarly distributed errors and a correctly specified linear mean; seasonality, store differences, or changing variance could make the stated coverage unreliable. The discount coefficient would still be an association unless a credible design supports a causal claim, and the interval should not be used for discount levels outside the observed range.
lessons.takeaway: Ask whether uncertainty concerns an average response or one new observation; the intervals answer different questions.
lessons.formula: Prediction uncertainty = mean-estimate uncertainty + new-observation noise; exact interval formulas depend on the fitted model.

lessons.title: Validate predictions on data the model did not see
lessons.body:
A model can fit its training sample yet fail on new periods. Split observations by a defensible design: for time-ordered finance data, train on earlier dates and test on later dates rather than randomly shuffling away temporal structure. Compare test-set metrics such as mean absolute error, which averages absolute prediction errors in outcome units, or root mean squared error, which emphasizes large errors. Inspect whether performance changes across calm and stressed periods. Cross-validation can help tune a model, but repeated tuning against the same test set leaks information. Include fees, timestamps, missingness and the information actually available at prediction time; a good score is not evidence of causality.

For a time-ordered test, calculate errors using only information available before each forecast. Suppose three synthetic test-month sales outcomes are 100, 120, and 80 units, while predictions are 90, 130, and 70 units. Absolute errors are |100−90| = 10, |120−130| = 10, and |80−70| = 10 units, so MAE = (10 + 10 + 10)/3 = 10 units per month. A random split could accidentally let a later market regime influence training, making this score look safer than a chronological test. The metric is on the outcome scale, so it is not 10 percent unless the outcome itself is defined as a percent. This comparison assumes test outcomes are measured consistently. Low MAE shows predictive performance in that test setting, not causality or guaranteed future accuracy. For residual diagnostics and validation practice, see ‘NIST — Residual Diagnostics’ in the linked sources.

A useful second check is to compare a model with a simple benchmark at each chronological forecast origin. Consider four illustrative, synthetic monthly fund excess returns (in percentage points), observed as 0.8, −0.2, 1.4, and −0.5. Suppose forecasts made without using the current month are 0.2, 0.2, 0.4, and −0.3, giving errors y − ŷ of 0.6, −0.4, 1.0, and −0.2 pp. The model’s MAE is (0.6 + 0.4 + 1.0 + 0.2)/4 = 0.55 pp, while its RMSE is √[(0.6² + (−0.4)² + 1.0² + (−0.2)²)/4] = √0.39 ≈ 0.62 pp. A zero-excess-return benchmark has MAE (0.8 + 0.2 + 1.4 + 0.5)/4 = 0.725 pp and RMSE √0.7225 = 0.85 pp, so this tiny test favors the model on both metrics. That comparison is descriptive, not proof of persistence: four months cannot characterize regimes, and the forecast must be formed before outcomes are known. If the decision concerns investable returns, evaluate net-of-fee outcomes separately; lower forecast error does not automatically imply profitable or causal trading advice.
lessons.takeaway: Out-of-sample validation estimates predictive usefulness, while design and assumptions determine whether causal claims are credible.
lessons.formula: MAE = (1/n)Σ|yᵢ − ŷᵢ|; n = number of test cases, yᵢ = observed outcome, ŷᵢ = prediction.

lessons.title: Association, prediction and causality in a finance example
lessons.body:
Consider a deliberately illustrative regression of a diversified fund's monthly excess return on the market's monthly excess return. With market returns −2%, 0%, 2% and fund returns −3%, 1%, 2%, both sample means are 0 percentage points. The sample covariance is 5 percentage-points-squared and market variance is 4, so the slope (often called beta) is b₁ = 5/4 = 1.25 fund percentage points per market percentage point. This tiny simulated sample shows co-movement, not a trading rule. Omitted exposures, fees, changing regimes and measurement choices remain. A regression association may help prediction, but changing the market is not a randomized intervention; causal interpretation needs design or strong identification assumptions.

In a synthetic example, a fund’s monthly excess return is 1 percentage point when the market’s excess return is 2 percentage points, and the fitted intercept is 0 percentage points with beta 0.8 fund percentage points per market percentage point. The fitted fund return is 0 + 0.8 × 2 = 1.6 percentage points, so the residual is 1.0 − 1.6 = −0.6 percentage points. The negative residual is a model error for that month, not a loss caused by the market. Beta summarizes average association over the chosen sample and may change with fees, exposures, or regimes. It does not say that forcing the market up by 1 percentage point would cause the fund to rise 0.8 points. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Angrist & Pischke (2008), Mostly Harmless Econometrics, Ch. 3, §§3.1–3.2.3’ in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, that a fitted monthly-return model is y-hat = 0.30 + 0.70x, where both fund excess return y and market excess return x are percentage points and the sample mean of x is 0. An illustrative month with x = 1.5 pp therefore has a fitted fund excess return of 0.30 + (0.70)(1.5) = 1.35 pp. To separate uncertainty about an average response from uncertainty for one fund return, assume the residual standard deviation is 1.50 pp, there are n = 36 months, and the centered predictor sum of squares is Sxx = 48 pp². The standard error for the mean response at x = 1.5 is 1.50√[1/36 + 1.5²/48] = 0.41 pp, giving an illustrative 95% mean-response interval of 1.35 ± 1.96(0.41), or 0.55 to 2.15 pp. For one future month, include the extra 1 inside the square root: 1.50√[1 + 1/36 + 1.5²/48] = 1.56 pp, so the approximate prediction interval is −1.70 to 4.40 pp. These calculations assume independent, constant-variance, approximately normal residuals; they describe association and prediction, not a causal market intervention, and can fail under regime changes or extrapolation.
lessons.takeaway: A coefficient can summarize historical association or aid prediction without proving what would happen under an intervention.
lessons.formula: b₁ = Cov(x,y)/Var(x); Cov = joint variation, Var = predictor variation, b₁ = slope in outcome units per x unit.

practice.question: In the illustrative example, what does beta = 1.25 mean, and what does it not prove?
practice.hint: Use the percentage-point units and distinguish association from intervention effects.
practice.solution: Within this tiny simulated sample and model, a 1 percentage-point market move is associated with 1.25 fund percentage points on average. It does not prove a causal effect or guarantee persistence.

caseStudy: An educational analyst regresses a diversified fund's monthly excess return on the market's monthly excess return over a clearly defined historical window. The slope, often called beta, describes average co-movement in fund percentage points per market percentage point; the intercept describes the fitted fund excess return when market excess return is zero. The analyst reports coefficient intervals, plots residuals against fitted values and time, checks changing volatility and influential observations, and compares chronological held-out prediction errors. If the market coefficient is statistically detectable, that still does not establish that market movements caused each fund return, that the effect is economically useful after fees, or that it will persist. A small illustrative or simulated dataset can teach the arithmetic but cannot support historical claims. Limitations include omitted factors, benchmark choice, nonstationary regimes, serial dependence, selection, data revisions and look-ahead bias. The exercise supports statistical reasoning, not investment advice or a forecast.
misconceptions: A high R-squared proves the model is right, causal or useful out of sample. It is only an in-sample fit summary under a particular calculation.
A statistically significant slope is automatically economically large or practically useful. Effect size, units, uncertainty, costs and context still matter.
A nonsignificant slope proves the true association is zero. It may reflect limited precision, high noise, low power or a misspecified model.
A fitted line predicts every next point closely. Individual outcomes vary, prediction intervals are wider, and extrapolation can be fragile.
Normal residuals or a good fit establish causation. Causal claims require design and identification assumptions beyond regression output.

quiz.question: What does an estimated slope in a regression of fund return on market return represent by itself?
options: A causal effect guaranteed in future months.
An estimated conditional association per unit of market return under the fitted model.
The proportion of observations correctly predicted.
quiz.explanation: Causal interpretation requires design and assumptions beyond fitting a regression line. The slope is expressed in outcome units per predictor unit and is conditional on the data, model and period used.
